S002.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
S002.description: Often has difficulty sustaining attention in tasks or play activities.
examples: Focuses at first during class or meetings but soon becomes distracted or spaces out.
Re-reads the same paragraph in a book multiple times but the content does not register.
Loses focus while watching movies or TV and misses the plot.
Unable to maintain attention until the end of a long meeting or lecture, often drifting off or becoming drowsy.

S008.name: Distractibility
S008.description: Often easily distracted by extraneous stimuli (for older adolescents and adults, may include unrelated thoughts).
examples: Easily distracted and stops working due to small noises or movements nearby.
Cannot concentrate because eyes keep wandering to the scenery outside the window or people passing by.
Starts daydreaming or gets sidetracked by sudden thoughts while working or studying.
Loses focus and listens in when hearing side conversations or TV sounds.

S009.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
S009.description: Often forgetful in daily activities (e.g., doing chores, running errands; for older adolescents and adults, returning calls, paying bills, keeping appointments).
examples: Forgets appointment times or meeting schedules, arriving late or missing them entirely.
Forgets to reply to received calls or messages for days.
Frequently incurs late fees because of missing deadlines for utility bills or credit card payments.
Forgets to take medication or leaves necessary items at home when going out.

S010.name: Fidgeting
S010.description: Often fidgets with or taps hands or feet or squirms in seat.
examples: Constantly shaking legs or twisting and squirming body while seated.
Spinning a pen or fiddling with nearby objects, unable to keep hands still.
Continually changing posture and feeling uncomfortable while sitting.
Constantly moving, such as tapping the desk with fingers or tapping feet on the floor.

S011.name: Leaving_Seat
S011.description: Often leaves seat in situations when remaining seated is expected.
examples: Frequently leaves seat or wanders around during class or meetings using excuses.
Unable to sit still during meals and keeps getting up.
Leaves seat in the middle of a movie or performance to go to the restroom or go outside.
Continually leaves seat and wanders around in the office where one is expected to sit and work.

S012.name: Feeling_Restless
S012.description: Often runs about or climbs in situations where it is inappropriate. (Note: In adolescents or adults, may be limited to feeling restless.)
examples: Feels uncomfortable and restless as if something is squirming inside when sitting still.
Feels internally anxious and stifled in situations requiring prolonged sitting.
A sense of urgency and anxiety that one must keep moving or doing something.
Feels unable to endure staying still and must constantly be doing something.

S013.name: Quiet_Activity_Difficulty
S013.description: Often unable to play or engage in leisure activities quietly.
examples: Unable to engage in calm activities for long, such as reading quietly or drawing.
Cannot play quietly, often shouting or making loud noises during games or play.
Unable to stay quiet in quiet places like libraries or movie theaters, making noise.
Cannot endure and avoids quiet and calm activities like meditation or yoga.

S015.name: Excessive_Talking
examples: Talks incessantly and cannot tolerate silence, continuing to chatter.
Continues to talk even when others are bored or try to cut the conversation short.
Talks too much inappropriately for the situation, making people around them uncomfortable.
Monopolizes the conversation and gives almost no chance for others to speak.

S018.name: Interrupting_Intruding
S018.description: Often interrupts or intrudes on others (e.g., butts into conversations, games, or activities).
examples: Butts into conversations of others where they have not been invited.
Joins in on others' work or games without permission or interferes.
Touches or uses other people's belongings or work without permission.
Keeps talking to and disturbing others when they are focusing on work or studying.

symptom.disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation) is characterized by a persistent pattern of hyperactivity and impulsivity that interferes with functioning or development, with inattention symptoms often present but not predominant. Clinically, individuals may present with chronic restlessness, difficulty remaining seated or engaging in quiet activities, excessive talking, and impulsive actions that lead to social, academic, or occupational impairment. Symptoms usually begin in childhood, but in some people they are only recognized or become clinically significant later in life when environmental demands change or compensatory strategies fail. It is distinguished from mood, anxiety, or personality disorders by its early onset, cross-situational persistence, and stable trait-like pattern of hyperactive/impulsive behavior rather than episodic or situationally bound disturbance.

patient.stressor: Marie had managed to get by in high school and early factory work by choosing hands‑on tasks and working alone, but about 14 months ago her plant upgraded to faster, more complex production lines and stricter safety protocols. As she moved into a technician role with hopes of promotion, she was expected to monitor multiple machines, respond to alarms, and sit through lengthy training sessions, all while maintaining flawless safety compliance and documentation. Her long‑standing tendency to act quickly and move from station to station became a liability: supervisors wrote her up for disrupting briefings, missing critical steps, and making impulsive adjustments that occasionally shut lines down, and she narrowly avoided a serious safety incident when she stepped into a restricted area without waiting for a lockout. After being put on a performance improvement plan and told that future certifications were at risk unless she could reliably stay focused and follow procedures, Marie sought psychiatric help at the urging of a union rep who wondered if there was an underlying attention disorder contributing to her escalating workplace problems.
patient.chief_complaint: “I can’t seem to stay focused on what I’m doing at the machines long enough to do the job the way they need me to.”
